1009.title: No water, no moon
1009.hook: the nun Chiyono's bucket bottom breaks, the moon's reflection vanishes, and she awakens
1009.howItsDone: Chiyono's story and her verse about the broken bucket are retold in Zen collections, alongside other stories of awakening that come in an ordinary moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ryokan, curled up in the straw at dawn. Your line was still hiding.

An old wooden bucket, its staves held together by a hoop of bamboo. A nun carries it out at night to fetch water. As she walks back she glances down: the full moon is floating in the water, bright and round, held right there in her bucket. Then the bamboo hoop snaps. The staves spring apart, the bottom drops out, and the water rushes onto the ground. The moon in the bucket is gone. Tradition says that in that moment, the nun Chiyono woke up.
screen: `THE MOON IN HER BUCKET.` → `THE HOOP SNAPS.` → `THE WATER IS GONE.`

segments.voice: Chiyono comes to us through Zen stories as a woman who practiced for a long time, working and sitting at a temple, without the breakthrough she hoped for. Tellings differ about her life before; they agree about the bucket. First, the moon in the water. Buddhist writing uses this picture for things that look solid and aren't. The moon in a bucket looks real; you could almost scoop it out. But it's a reflection, lasting only as long as the water stays still and the bucket holds. Second, the bottom falls out. Tradition gives Chiyono a short verse about that night. In plain English it says, roughly: I tried this way and that to keep the old bucket together, until the bottom fell out. Where no water stays, no moon lives. Read that way, her years of effort were the bamboo hoop, holding things together: the bucket, the practice, the picture of what awakening should look like. When the hoop gave way, what she'd held so carefully turned out not to be what she was looking for. Third, what's not lost. The story never says the moon left the sky. Only the copy went, with the water. Some readers hear the self in that bucket, a reflection carried carefully from place to place. Others hear every idea of awakening, which has to spill before awakening can happen. The story leaves room for both, and the real moon stays where it always was.
screen: `CHIYONO AND THE OLD BUCKET.` · `THE MOON IN THE WATER.` · `THE BOTTOM FALLS OUT.` · `ONLY THE REFLECTION IS GONE.`

segments.voice: If there's a glass near you, pour a little into another cup or a sink and watch it go; if not, remember rain sliding off a roof, or a wave pulling back from the sand. Notice the moment the water leaves its shape. Then let each out-breath spill the same way, holding nothing together.
No water. Chiyono's bucket breaks, the water spills, and the moon's reflection is gone, while the moon itself stays in the sky. Today's word.
Your line: the bottom fell out. What spilled was only water, never the moon. Until tomorrow.

1010.title: Lay meditation
1010.hook: Ledi Sayadaw in Burma teaches meditation to laypeople, not only monks
1010.howItsDone: In Theravada countries and beyond, lay Buddhists now attend meditation retreats and centers, and some lineages trace this lay practice back through teachers such as Ledi Sayadaw and Saya Thetgyi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chiyono's bucket, the bottom falling out under the moon. Your line was the bottom fell out.

Who is meditation for? In Burma, in Ledi Sayadaw's day, the usual answer, as accounts tell it, was the monks. Lay people offered food, kept the precepts, made merit, and left the long hours of sitting to those in robes. Ledi Sayadaw, a learned monk, started giving a different answer. Farmers could do this. Shopkeepers could. Parents with no spare time could. He wrote short guides in plain Burmese and sent them out into the towns and villages.
screen: `WHO IS MEDITATION FOR?` → `THE MONKS, MOSTLY.` → `LEDI SAYS: EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: First, the worry behind it. Accounts describe a teacher afraid the practice could shrink into something people only read about, kept alive by a few. His answer was to put it in more hands, not fewer. Second, the tools. His practical guides, in the language people actually spoke, covered keeping attention on the breath and seeing body and mind change from moment to moment. The Pali word for that seeing is vipassana: insight, seeing clearly. It wasn't a new teaching; the instructions on mindfulness of breathing and of the body are in the old suttas. What was new was who he handed them to. Third, the farmer. A story told in this lineage: a rice farmer named Saya Thetgyi learned from Ledi and became a teacher himself, a lay man teaching lay people in his own village. From him the teaching passed through other lay teachers, and teachers in this line say it now reaches meditation halls far from Burma, where lay people of every kind sit side by side. Fourth, what changed and what didn't. Ledi didn't set monastic life aside; he stayed a monk. He simply said the door was wider than people thought. Sitting wasn't a reward for leaving the world. It was something to carry into it, between the fields and the market, between one chore and the next.
screen: `A FEAR THE PRACTICE WOULD SHRINK.` · `PLAIN GUIDES IN PLAIN BURMESE.` · `A FARMER BECOMES A TEACHER.` · `THE DOOR IS WIDER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, breathe through the nose, and notice the touch of the air just at the nostrils as it comes in and as it goes out; that's the whole instruction. When the mind wanders off, come back to the touch. Keep it simple enough that you could explain it to anyone in one sentence.
Lay meditation. Ledi Sayadaw's teaching that insight practice belongs to farmers and shopkeepers as well as monks. Today's word.
Your line: for everyone. The door was wider than people thought. That's day one thousand ten.

1011.title: Noting spreads
1011.hook: Mahasi Sayadaw's method of noting travels far beyond Burma
1011.howItsDone: In Mahasi-style retreats, meditators alternate periods of sitting, noting the rise and fall of the abdomen, with slow walking, noting each part of each step, often for whole days in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lay meditation: Ledi Sayadaw opening insight practice to farmers and shopkeepers. Your line was for everyone.

Rising. Falling. Rising. Falling. Two words, said silently, over and over, in a meditation hall in Burma or on another continent. A person sits, sometimes with a hand on the belly. As the belly lifts with the in-breath: rising. As it sinks: falling. A sound from outside. Hearing, hearing. An itch on the cheek. Itching. A sudden memory of breakfast. Thinking. Then back to the belly. That's the method a Burmese monk, Mahasi Sayadaw, taught.
screen: `RISING. FALLING.` → `HEARING, HEARING.` → `THINKING. BACK TO THE BELLY.`

segments.voice: First, the home base. Mahasi built his teaching on the old instructions of the Satipatthana Sutta, to be mindful of body, feelings, mind and the things the mind meets. He made the start simple: one place to return to, the rise and fall of the belly, again and again. Second, the label. Whatever pulls attention away gets a plain word, not a judgment or a story, just a name for what's happening: hearing, itching, wanting, worrying. The note is made silently, and teachers in his line describe it as light, a whisper rather than a shout. Naming a sound as hearing keeps you from building a whole argument about the neighbor's car; the label catches the moment before the story starts. Third, walking. In Mahasi centers, practice doesn't stop when you stand up. Students walk slowly back and forth, noting each step: lifting, moving, placing. They alternate sitting and walking through the day, so attention carries from the cushion to the floor to the dining hall. Fourth, how it traveled. Mahasi's students, monks and lay people both, carried the method to centers in other countries, and teachers there adapted it. Some keep careful labels for everything; some use them only when the mind gets lost. Plain enough to travel and flexible enough to change: that's how rising, falling came to be whispered in halls a long way from where Mahasi taught.
screen: `A HOME BASE: RISING, FALLING.` · `A SOFT LABEL, NOT A JUDGMENT.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `PLAIN ENOUGH TO TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Find the movement of your belly as you breathe, resting a hand there if it helps, and silently note rising as it lifts and falling as it sinks. When something pulls you away, give it one soft word, hearing, thinking, itching, planning, then come back to rising, falling. No need to note perfectly, or to note everything; a whisper is enough.
Noting spreads. Mahasi Sayadaw's method: rising, falling, and a soft label for whatever pulls you away, carried by his students far beyond Burma. Today's word.
Your line: rising, falling. One plain word can catch the moment. Day one thousand eleven.

1012.title: The forest wanderer
1012.hook: Ajahn Mun walks the Thai forests, reviving the strict forest life
1012.howItsDone: Monks in the Thai forest tradition live in forest monasteries, walk for alms each morning, and some take on the dhutanga practices, sometimes wandering for a season in what Thai Buddhists call thudong.

segments.voice: Yesterday, noting spreads: Mahasi Sayadaw's soft labels. Your line was rising, falling.

Dawn under a tree. A monk climbs out from beneath a cloth umbrella hung from a branch, a net around it against the mosquitoes. He shoulders his bowl and walks barefoot into the nearest village, where people put rice in it. He takes what's given, walks back into the trees, and eats once. Then he sits, and walks, and sits. In a few days or weeks he'll move on to another forest, and another. The stories told about him mention wild animals, fever and long nights of fear. His name was Ajahn Mun.
screen: `A NET, A BOWL, A TREE.` → `ONE MEAL, THEN BACK TO THE FOREST.` → `ALWAYS MOVING ON.`

segments.voice: First, what he took on. The Pali tradition describes a set of strict practices, dhutanga, that a monk may choose: living in the forest, eating only food received on alms round, eating from the bowl alone, wearing robes of cast-off cloth, sleeping at the foot of a tree. They're optional; tradition says the Buddha praised them and refused to make them required. Ajahn Mun chose them and kept them, and that's what people mean when they say he revived the forest life in Thailand. Second, why the forest. There's no comfort to hide in. When fear comes at night, you sit with fear. When hunger comes, you sit with hunger. Accounts written by his students tell of fear met with steady meditation until it passed. The forest wasn't scenery. It was the teacher that wouldn't let him look away. Third, the students. Monks who wanted to train with him had to find him first, and he kept moving. Those who caught up learned as much from watching as from talks: how he walked, ate, swept and sat. The Thai forest teachers who came after him speak of him as a root teacher. Fourth, what wandering meant. Not running away, but keeping nothing: no fixed hut to defend, no reputation to manage, no comfortable corner. Just the next step, the bowl, and the mind as it is right now.
screen: `DHUTANGA: STRICT PRACTICES, CHOSEN.` · `NO COMFORT TO HIDE IN.` · `STUDENTS HAD TO FIND HIM.` · `A WAY OF KEEPING NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Stand near a tree, or a window with a tree in view, or bring one to mind, and walk a few slow steps or simply stand still. Let your attention widen and listen to whatever is around you as if it were forest sound: wind, a bird, a far-off engine. If restlessness or a little fear shows up, let it walk with you.
Dhutanga. The strict practices a monk may choose, like living in the forest and eating once a day, which Ajahn Mun kept. Today's word.
Your line: just the next step. No hut to defend, only the bowl and the mind. See you tomorrow.

1013.title: A forest student
1013.hook: Ajahn Chah, Ajahn Mun's student in spirit, whose forest monastery welcomed Western monks
1013.howItsDone: Monasteries in Ajahn Chah's lineage, in Thailand and in other countries, follow the forest routine of alms round, work and meditation, and welcome lay visitors and guests who wish to stay and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ajahn Mun, with his bowl and a tree for a roof. Your line was just the next step.

A young man from the West stands at the gate of a forest monastery in Thailand, newly ordained or hoping to be. He doesn't speak the language. He doesn't know the chants. He isn't sure how to wrap a robe or where to leave his sandals. The teacher could easily tell him to come back when he knows more. Instead, as the story is told, he's let in and put to work: sweeping leaves off the paths, hauling water, walking for alms with everyone else. The teacher was Ajahn Chah.
screen: `A STRANGER AT THE GATE.` → `NO LANGUAGE, NO CHANTS.` → `LET IN AND HANDED A BROOM.`

segments.voice: First, a student in spirit. Tradition says Ajahn Chah spent only a short time with Ajahn Mun, yet that meeting stayed with him. Afterward he wandered and practiced in the forests the way Mun had, and in time settled in a forest near his home village, where a monastery grew up around him. Not long years at Mun's side, but the same forest way. Second, his teaching. Accounts describe him speaking in plain village language, with jokes and everyday pictures: a glass of muddy water settling, a leaf stirred by the wind. When students complained about the heat, the food or each other, he'd turn the complaint around. The trouble, he suggested, wasn't the heat. It was the wanting it to be different. Third, the welcome. Western monks came, and he didn't build them an easier track. They ate the same food, kept the same hours, swept the same paths and sat through the same restless nights. In time a monastery was set up near his own, Wat Pah Nanachat, where newcomers from abroad could train with teaching in English. Fourth, what welcome means here. Not lowering the bar, but opening the gate and walking beside the newcomer through the same hard days. The forest welcomed them, and it didn't change for them. Monasteries started later by his Western students carry the same pattern into other countries.
screen: `A STUDENT IN SPIRIT.` · `PLAIN WORDS, VILLAGE PICTURES.` · `NO SEPARATE, EASIER TRACK.` · `AN OPEN GATE, THE SAME PATH.`

segments.voice: Bring back a time you were the newcomer, at a job, a school, a family dinner where you knew nobody, and remember what helped: someone who showed you where things were, someone who didn't make you feel slow. Breathe with that memory for a moment. Then hold in mind someone who's new in your life right now, for a few easy breaths.
Acariya. The Pali word for teacher, the root of the Thai title ajahn, given to teachers like Ajahn Chah who welcomed students from abroad. Today's word.
Your line: the forest welcomed them. An open gate, and the same path for all. Day one thousand thirteen, done.

1014.title: The garden of liberation
1014.hook: Buddhadasa's forest monastery in southern Thailand and his plain teaching
1014.howItsDone: Suan Mokkh still welcomes visitors and holds meditation retreats, and Buddhadasa's talks, published in plain Thai, are read by Thai Buddhists and in translation elsewhere.

segments.voice: Yesterday, acariya, the forest student: Ajahn Chah opening the gate to newcomers. Your line was the forest welcomed them.

Books packed, a monk who has been studying in Bangkok heads home. Not in defeat. He's decided the big city temples, with their exams and ranks, aren't where he'll find what he's looking for. Back in the south of Thailand, near the town he grew up in, he settles in a quiet, overgrown patch of forest and names it Suan Mokkh, the garden of liberation. He's known as Buddhadasa, and he wanted to talk about the Buddha's teaching in words anyone, a farmer, a student, a clerk, could use that afternoon.
screen: `HE LEAVES THE CITY TEMPLES.` → `A QUIET FOREST IN THE SOUTH.` → `SUAN MOKKH: THE GARDEN OF LIBERATION.`

segments.voice: First, two languages. Buddhadasa taught that religious words can be heard two ways. There's everyday language, the words as people usually take them, and there's what he called Dhamma language, the same words heard inwardly. Rebirth, in everyday language, can mean being born again after death. In Dhamma language, he said, it can also mean the self being born again and again in the mind, every time we grab hold of I and mine. He didn't tell people to throw the first meaning away; he asked them to hear the second too. Second, plain words. He spoke to farmers, officials and students in ordinary Thai. At Suan Mokkh he put teachings on signs among the trees and paintings on the walls, so a visitor could learn just by walking around. Third, cooling, here and now. The old texts picture nibbana as a fire going out. Buddhadasa liked the picture of cooling, and taught that a taste of it can come in ordinary life, whenever grasping drops for a moment, not only at the end of a long road. Fourth, not everyone agreed. Some Thai Buddhists felt his readings went too far from the traditional ones; others found them freeing. He kept teaching plainly, and the signs among the trees stayed up for anyone who walked in, a farmer or a professor, to read on the way past.
screen: `EVERYDAY LANGUAGE, DHAMMA LANGUAGE.` · `SIGNS AMONG THE TREES.` · `COOLING, HERE AND NOW.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you understand well, how to cook rice, why you love a certain song, a rule of a game, and explain it in your head as if to a curious child: short words, one picture, no showing off. Notice where you reach for a fancy word, and swap it for a plain one. Then let the breath be plain too: in, and out.
Buddhadasa. The Thai monk who taught the Buddha's teaching in plain words at his forest monastery, Suan Mokkh, the garden of liberation. Today's word.
Your line: plain words. The same old words, heard inwardly too. That's day one thousand fourteen.

1015.title: Ambedkar's conversion
1015.hook: at Nagpur, Dr B. R. Ambedkar and a great crowd of Dalits take refuge
1015.howItsDone: Ambedkarite Buddhists mark the anniversary of the Nagpur conversion each year, and crowds gather at the site in Nagpur, now called Deekshabhoomi, to take the refuges and remember Ambedkar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddhadasa's forest garden and his two languages. Your line was plain words.

An open ground in Nagpur, a city in the middle of India, and a great crowd stretching back across it. In the crowd are Dalits, people the caste system had called untouchable: kept from common wells, from temple doors, from classrooms. At the front stands a lawyer and scholar, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, who helped draft the constitution of independent India and spent his life fighting caste discrimination. Today he isn't here to argue a case. He's here to take refuge in the Buddha.
screen: `AN OPEN GROUND IN NAGPUR.` → `A CROWD OF DALITS.` → `AMBEDKAR AT THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, his own life. Ambedkar was born into a Dalit family. Accounts of his childhood say he had to sit apart at school and couldn't drink from the common water unless someone poured it for him. He studied anyway, in India and abroad, and became a lawyer, an economist and a leader of his people. Second, a long search. Long before this day, he had said publicly that he would leave the religion he was born into, and he studied more than one path before choosing. He chose the Buddha's, for his own reasons: a teaching that, as he read it, rested on reason, compassion and the equal worth of every person. This is his story and his reading, told here as his. Hindus have their own and varied answers to caste, and Hindu reformers have fought untouchability too. Third, the ceremony. Accounts say Ambedkar first received the refuges and precepts himself from a senior Buddhist monk. Then he turned to the crowd and led them through the refuges in Pali, line by line: Buddham saranam gacchami, I go to the Buddha for refuge; then the Dhamma; then the Sangha. A whole field of voices repeating after one. Fourth, the week. Chiyono's bucket, the water gone and the moon still in the sky. Ledi Sayadaw opening meditation to everyone. Mahasi's rising, falling. Ajahn Mun in the forests, Ajahn Chah at the gate, Buddhadasa's plain words. And today, on an open ground, a crowd that had been refused dignity for generations stands up and chooses it.
screen: `BORN DALIT, KEPT FROM THE WATER.` · `A LONG SEARCH, HIS OWN REASONS.` · `HE TAKES REFUGE, THEN LEADS IT.` · `A WEEK OF TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone, from your family, your history or your neighborhood, who had to fight to be treated as fully human: to learn, to vote, to be served, to be heard. Hold their face or their name for a few breaths. You don't need to say anything; just let them be honored for a moment, here, in you.
Ambedkar's conversion. At Nagpur, Dr. B. R. Ambedkar takes refuge in the Buddha, then leads a great crowd of Dalits through the refuges. Today's word.
Your line: dignity chosen. Refuge, taken together by a whole field of voices. Day one thousand fifteen.
